title: Indoor soundscape assessment: A principal components model of acoustic perception in residential buildings
research_question: The study aimed (i) to define and analyze the dimensions underlying acoustic perception in indoor residential living rooms and (ii) to discuss the potential implications of such a model for building design practice.

participants.description: 32 participants (17 females, 18 males, mean age: 31.7 years, SD: 7.2 years), university students and researchers, self-reported no hearing impairment and good English level, from London, UK.
participants.recruitment: invited via adverts on social media and email

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 20 unique 1-minute audio scenarios, each combining one of five outdoor urban contexts (no added sound, heavy traffic, light traffic, pedestrian area, garden) with one of four indoor sound sources (fan noise, music, TV, no added sound). Audio excerpts were reproduced at measured in situ LAeq,1min levels.

A mock-up living room (3.49m width, 3.35m length, 3.16m height) furnished with an armchair, lounge table, plant, and a television. A curtain was hung at 0.95m from the front wall to integrate a 55" display projecting a window view. Reverberation time (T30,500Hz-2kHz) was 0.13s.

measures.construct: Affective response to indoor soundscapes (perceptual dimensions)
measures.instrument: 97 unidirectional attribute scales (Semantic Differentials) rated on visual analog scales (0-100, 'No match at all' to 'Perfect match')
LAeq,1min (A-weighted equivalent continuous sound pressure level), N10 (loudness exceeded 10% of the time) calculated from binaural recordings using ArtemiS SUITE V.10

LA10-LA90 (difference between 10% and 90% statistical levels of A-weighted equivalent continuous sound pressure level), N10-N90 (loudness difference), Fluctuation Strength (FS), Roughness (R) calculated from binaural recordings using ArtemiS SUITE V.10
LC-LA (difference between C and A-weighted sound pressure level), Sharpness (S) calculated from binaural recordings using ArtemiS SUITE V.10

The negative relationship between loudness and comfort persisted even when accounting for sound categories, suggesting a fundamental impact of sound magnitude.
Natural sounds contribute positively to comfort, aligning with theories of biophilia and stress recovery.

mechanisms: Semantic meaning of sounds: The inclusion of sound categories (semantic features) significantly improved the prediction of perceptual dimensions (Comfort, Content, Familiarity) beyond objective acoustic parameters alone.
Informational properties of sounds: Sound categories provide informational cues that influence perception.
Perceived noise control: The 'Privacy and Control' dimension relates to the ability to manage one's acoustic environment, which is a key aspect of home as a private space.
Interference with desired sounds: Detrimental effects on comfort (e.g., light traffic with music/TV) are attributed to interference with music enjoyment or speech intelligibility.
moderators: Outdoor urban context (Factor A: no added sound, heavy traffic, light traffic, pedestrian area, garden)
Indoor sound source (Factor B: fan noise, music, TV, no added sound)
implementation_implications: The proposed model provides a reference for indoor soundscape research and practice, indicating which perceptual constructs and attribute scales to measure in buildings.
POE surveys should integrate soundscape methodologies to assess sound impact on Comfort, Content, Engagement, Privacy, Control, and Familiarity, moving beyond just annoyance.
Design interventions can be guided by plotting existing and target soundscapes in the perceptual space (Comfort-Content) to assess their effectiveness.
Ventilation devices can be reinterpreted as systems to transmit, block, or adjust external sounds to provide connection with the outside, release wanted sounds, and mask unwanted sounds.
Acoustic design requirements should evolve beyond noise level limits to consider soundscape quality.
Predictive indices based on the proposed model can be developed to guide the design stage.

limitations: The number of tested exposure conditions (n=20) in relation to the number of variables (p=97) for PCA, which ideally relies on larger sample sizes for stability.

The study was limited to relaxing tasks (e.g., reading, watching TV, listening to music) and did not investigate more cognitively demanding tasks or situations with extremely full content (e.g., party).
The model does not apply to bedrooms where sleep disturbance is a primary concern.
Factors such as the sound of neighbors, building features, urban context, personality traits, socio-economic, situational, and environmental factors were not included and require future research.
